title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 23–24
description: Curated geographical terminology, place-name article patterns, environmental vocabulary, conservation expressions and B2 word families.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Study tables, geographic diagrams and labels, language-help notes, usage contrasts, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical and grammatical coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Selected broad British IPA for checked words and concise expressions; uncertain long expressions omit IPA. Local accent and connected-speech variants are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Comparison with the study and illustrated teaching pages, exercises and answer key; linguistic, provenance, spelling, audio-target and structural checks. Live app import and browser speech recognition were not tested.
audit.limitations: Audio paths are intentionally empty because no recordings are bundled; browser TTS and speech-recognition depend on installed voices and were not tested live.

units.title: Unit 23 — Physical geography
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 23. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Use the definite article correctly with countries, islands, mountain ranges, rivers, seas and other geographical names.
Describe landscapes with accurate vocabulary for plains, volcanoes, ice fields, springs and geysers.
Distinguish coastal, river and mountain features such as shore, peninsula, estuary, tributary, gorge and ridge.
Use natural geographical adjective–noun combinations and distinguish near-synonyms by physical meaning.

items.example: The map identifies the main geographical features of the region.
items.note: A natural landform or physical feature; the adjective geographical refers to geography.

items.example: France is a country in western Europe.
items.note: Most country names take no the, but plural country names such as the Philippines take the.

items.example: Mount Kenya is an important landmark in East Africa.
items.note: Individual mountain names generally have no the: Mount Everest, not the Mount Everest.

items.example: The Alps are a well-known mountain range in Europe.
items.note: Names of mountain chains (also called mountain ranges) usually take the: the Alps or the Himalayas.

items.example: Sicily is an island in the Mediterranean Sea.
items.note: Individual island names usually have no the; the s in island is silent.

items.example: The West Indies are a group of islands in the Caribbean.
items.note: Names for groups of islands usually take the, unlike single-island names.

items.example: The River Thames flows through London.
items.note: River names generally take the: the Thames, the Volga or the River Amazon.

items.example: The Pacific Ocean is larger than the Atlantic Ocean.
items.note: Names of oceans normally take the.

items.example: The Mediterranean Sea has a long coastline.
items.note: Names of seas generally take the, as in the Mediterranean.

items.example: The Gulf of Mexico receives water from several rivers.
items.note: Names of gulfs generally take the.

items.example: The fishing boats sheltered in a small bay.
items.note: Named bays often take the, as in the Bay of Biscay; a bay is a broad inlet along a coast.

items.example: A narrow strait separates the two islands.
items.note: A narrow stretch of water between landmasses; named straits generally take the.

items.example: Lake Erie lies on the border between the United States and Canada.
items.note: Names beginning with Lake usually have no the: Lake Erie, not the Lake Erie.

items.example: A strong current carried the small boat away from shore.
items.note: A flow of water in a particular direction; names of major currents take the.

items.example: The Gulf Stream carries warm water across the North Atlantic.
items.note: A named ocean current; keep the definite article in ordinary use.

items.example: The Japan of today is different from the country described in that old book.
items.note: Even a country name that normally takes no article can take the when qualified by a limiting phrase.

items.example: The mountain landscape looked different after the snowfall.
items.note: The visible physical features of an area; can include both natural and human elements.

items.example: The island republic depends heavily on maritime trade.
items.note: A republic occupying one or more islands; the source uses Iceland as an example.

items.example: The region consists of low hills and broad valleys.
items.note: Consist of names the parts making up something; do not add a passive be before consist.

items.example: The hikers crossed a barren landscape with very little vegetation.
items.note: Land on which little grows; often used with land, plain or hillside.

items.example: A wide plain stretches towards the distant mountains.
items.note: A large relatively flat area of land; a plain is not necessarily infertile.

items.example: Few crops grow on the barren plains in this part of the island.
items.note: A descriptive adjective–noun pairing used for land where little vegetation grows.

items.example: The expedition crossed an ice field in the mountains.
items.note: A large continuous area of ice, distinct from a moving glacier.

items.example: A volcano rises above the nearby village.
items.note: Plural volcanoes; a mountain or opening from which magma and gases may escape.

items.example: Scientists are monitoring an active volcano on the island.
items.note: A volcano that is erupting or may erupt again; contrast with an extinct volcano.

items.example: The volcano could erupt without much warning.
items.note: Used when a volcano releases lava, ash or gas; often intransitive.

items.example: Visitors can bathe in a natural thermal spring.
items.note: A spring heated geothermally; hot spring is a common alternative.

items.example: The geyser sends hot water into the air every few hours.
items.note: A natural vent that periodically ejects hot water and steam; British pronunciation may vary.

items.example: Farmers choose crops that can survive a dry summer.
items.note: A plant grown as food or another agricultural product; often plural crops.

items.example: The western coast is exposed to strong Atlantic winds.
items.note: Land next to the sea, not normally a lake; compare shore.

items.example: We walked along the shore of the lake.
items.note: The land bordering a sea, lake or large body of water; broader than coast.

items.example: The children played on a sandy beach.
items.note: A strip of sand or pebbles beside the sea or a lake.

items.example: The path runs along the edge of a steep cliff.
items.note: A high, steep rock face, often near the coast.

items.example: A lighthouse stands on the cape overlooking the sea.
items.note: A point of land extending into the sea; the word also has an unrelated clothing meaning.

items.example: The town occupies a small peninsula between two bays.
items.note: Land almost surrounded by water but connected to a larger landmass.

items.example: The village has a sandy beach sheltered from the wind.
items.note: A natural adjective–noun combination used in the exercise.

items.example: Much of the rocky coast is inaccessible by road.
items.note: A natural combination for a coastline dominated by rock.

items.example: The river valley becomes narrower further upstream.
items.note: A useful collocation based on the textbook target valley.

items.example: Mist settled in the valley before sunrise.
items.note: Low land between hills or mountains, often with a river running through it.

items.example: A deep gorge cuts through the rocky plateau.
items.note: A narrow valley with very steep sides; not identical to a broad valley.

items.example: A clear stream runs behind the farmhouse.
items.note: A small river; shallow streams can still flow quickly.

items.example: The source of the river lies high in the mountains.
items.note: The place where a river begins; source has other non-geographical uses.

items.example: The waterfall drops into a narrow gorge.
items.note: A place where flowing water falls over a steep drop.

items.example: A small tributary joins the main river near the town.
items.note: A stream or smaller river that flows into a larger river.

items.example: The river widens considerably near its mouth.
items.note: The place where a river enters the sea, a lake or another water body; not the same as its source.

items.example: The river forms a broad delta before entering the sea.
items.note: Deposited sediment can form a region of branching channels near a river mouth.

items.example: Ships travel through the estuary towards the port.
items.note: A tidal river mouth where freshwater and seawater mix; it is not necessarily a delta.

items.example: We crossed a shallow stream on stepping stones.
items.note: The adjective shallow describes water of limited depth.

items.pt: rio turbulento; rio de águas agitadas
items.example: After the storm, the turbulent river was unsafe to cross.
items.note: Turbulent water moves violently or irregularly.

items.example: A small village stands at the foot of the mountain.
items.note: Foot is the lowermost part of a mountain; the fixed pattern is at the foot of.

items.example: The climbers followed a narrow ridge towards the summit.
items.note: A long narrow high section of a mountain, different from a single peak.

items.example: Snow covered the highest peak in the range.
items.note: A pointed or prominent top of a mountain; often interchangeable with summit in general contexts.

items.example: The team finally reached the summit before noon.
items.note: The highest point of a mountain; commonly used with reach the summit.

items.example: The glacier moves slowly down the mountainside.
items.note: A large mass of land ice flowing under its own weight, unlike a stationary ice field.

items.example: The bridge spans a steep gorge above the river.
items.note: Steep describes a sharply sloping hillside, cliff or gorge.

units.title: Unit 24 — Environmental problems
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 24. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Discuss major environmental threats and their causes using precise compounds and scientific terminology.
Distinguish climate change, global warming, greenhouse effect and ozone depletion.
Describe conservation, responsible waste handling and ways to reduce a carbon footprint.
Use the over- prefix and the word families of globalisation, environment, pollution, destruction, disposal and reduction.

items.example: Water scarcity is a serious environmental problem in some areas.
items.note: A difficulty affecting the natural environment; often plural environmental problems.

items.example: Globalisation has increased the exchange of goods and ideas.
items.note: Growing international economic, cultural and social connections; British spelling -sation.

items.example: Acid rain can damage lakes, forests and historic buildings.
items.note: Rain made unusually acidic by airborne pollutants, often linked to burning fossil fuels.

items.example: Air pollution is worse near heavily congested roads.
items.note: Contamination of air by harmful substances.

items.example: Untreated industrial waste can cause severe water pollution.
items.note: Contamination of rivers, lakes, oceans or other water sources.

items.example: Global warming is raising average temperatures over time.
items.note: Long-term increase in the Earth's average surface temperature; related to but not identical to climate change.

items.example: The laboratory follows strict rules for hazardous waste.
items.note: Waste that can threaten health or the environment; hazardous means dangerous.

items.example: International agreements have helped limit ozone depletion.
items.note: The thinning of stratospheric ozone; a distinct issue from global warming.

items.example: The ozone layer helps absorb harmful ultraviolet radiation.
items.note: A region of the stratosphere containing ozone that protects life from much of the Sun's UV radiation.

items.example: Heavy smog made it difficult to see the skyline.
items.note: Polluted haze, often a mixture of smoke, gases and fog-like conditions; the term comes from smoke and fog.

items.example: Rapid overpopulation can place pressure on housing and water supplies.
items.note: A situation in which the population exceeds what local resources and systems can sustainably support.

items.example: Rainforest destruction reduces habitats for many species.
items.note: Loss or clearing of tropical rainforests; also destruction of rainforests.

items.example: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warmer than it would otherwise be.
items.note: A natural atmospheric warming process that human greenhouse-gas emissions can intensify; not inherently a problem.

items.example: Carbon dioxide levels rise when large amounts of fossil fuel are burned.
items.note: CO2 is one of the greenhouse gases, distinct from carbon monoxide, CO.

items.example: Some gases remain in the atmosphere for many years.
items.note: The mixture of gases surrounding Earth.

items.example: The equipment measures the concentration of a gas in the air.
items.note: A substance in a gaseous state; plural gases.

items.example: Changes in the polar ice caps are monitored by satellites.
items.note: Large masses of ice covering polar regions; avoid confusing sea ice with land-based ice sheets.

items.example: The snow began to thaw when spring arrived.
items.note: To become unfrozen or the process of thawing; the source uses thawing of polar ice caps.

items.example: Climate change affects both rainfall patterns and average temperatures.
items.note: Long-term shifts in climate, not limited to temperature increases.

items.example: Several species depend on this wetland for survival.
items.note: Species is both singular and plural: one species, many species.

items.example: An endangered animal needs protection from further habitat loss.
items.note: At serious risk of extinction; often in endangered species.

items.example: The reserve helps protect endangered species.
items.note: A common expression; species has the same form in singular and plural.

items.example: Some species have already become extinct.
items.note: No longer existing anywhere; stronger than endangered.

items.example: Overfishing has reduced stocks of some commercially valuable fish.
items.note: The prefix over- indicates too much; unsustainable levels of fishing.

items.example: The coastal city has become severely overpopulated.
items.note: Describes a place with too many people for available resources and services.

items.example: Worldwide efforts to protect marine ecosystems have grown.
items.note: Worldwide is an adjective or adverb meaning around the world.

items.example: The green party proposed stricter pollution controls.
items.note: A political party emphasising environmental protection; not a specific party name here.

items.example: The council introduced green policies to reduce waste.
items.note: Policies intended to protect the environment; green is an adjective here.

items.example: Ecological policies can help restore damaged wetlands.
items.note: Environmental policy focusing on living organisms and their relationships with surroundings.

items.example: Conservation programmes have improved protection of the forest.
items.note: Protection and careful management of nature and resources.

items.example: A conservation organisation purchased land for wildlife protection.
items.note: An organisation whose work includes conserving habitats or species; UK spelling organisation.

items.example: The nature reserve provides a safe habitat for rare birds.
items.note: An area formally protected to conserve wildlife or habitats.

items.example: The school buys organic food from local producers.
items.note: Food produced in line with organic standards; do not equate organic with necessarily pesticide-free.

items.pt: ecologicamente correto; de menor impacto ambiental
items.example: Reusable containers can be more environmentally friendly than single-use packaging.
items.note: Causing less environmental harm; often hyphenated before a noun.

items.example: The restoration plan is designed to be ecologically sound.
items.note: Environmentally responsible according to ecological principles; not a guarantee of zero impact.

items.example: Please dispose of waste in the containers provided.
items.note: Dispose of requires of before the thing discarded; do not say dispose waste.

items.example: Our office recycles paper and metal packaging.
items.note: Process materials so that they can be used again; distinct from reusing an object unchanged.

items.example: Recycling can reduce the amount of rubbish sent to landfill.
items.note: The process or activity of converting waste into reusable material.

items.example: Flying less can help reduce your carbon footprint.
items.note: An estimate of greenhouse-gas emissions attributable to an activity, product or person.

items.example: Taking the train may reduce your carbon footprint on some journeys.
items.note: A common verb–noun combination; can also use lower or cut your carbon footprint.

items.example: The city aims to use fewer fossil fuels for public transport.
items.note: Coal, oil and natural gas are typical fossil fuels.

items.example: We are trying to cut down on unnecessary car journeys.
items.note: Phrasal verb meaning reduce the amount or frequency of something; keep the preposition on.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Digital platforms can globalise the reach of a small business.
items.note: Verb corresponding to globalisation; British spelling -ise.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The report describes a global problem.
items.note: Adjective meaning worldwide; related to globalisation.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The data were collected globally over several years.
items.note: Adverb formed from global.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The factory must meet standards that protect the environment.
items.note: The natural world and surroundings that may be affected by human activity.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The environmentalist spoke about protecting wetlands.
items.note: A person actively concerned with environmental protection.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: They commissioned an environmental assessment.
items.note: Adjective related to the environment; often before impact, damage or policy.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The project must be environmentally responsible.
items.note: Adverb used with friendly, sustainable and responsible.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Pollution from traffic has fallen since the new rules began.
items.note: Uncountable in its general environmental sense.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The filter removes a harmful pollutant from the air.
items.note: A substance or agent causing pollution; countable.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Untreated chemicals can pollute groundwater.
items.note: Verb: to contaminate air, water or land.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Older vehicles can be more polluting than newer ones.
items.note: Adjective or participle describing something that produces pollution.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The destruction of natural habitats threatens wildlife.
items.note: Noun corresponding to the verb destroy.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: A severe fire can destroy nesting sites.
items.note: Verb: to damage something so badly that it no longer exists or functions.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Some industrial practices are highly destructive.
items.note: Adjective describing something that causes major damage.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The machine can operate destructively if it is used incorrectly.
items.note: Adverb corresponding to destructive; less common in everyday conversation.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Safe disposal of batteries is important.
items.note: The act of getting rid of something; frequently waste disposal.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Staff must dispose of chemical waste safely.
items.note: Use dispose of + object in the sense of discarding something.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Disposable cups create unnecessary waste.
items.note: Intended to be used once or for a short time and then thrown away.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The policy led to a significant reduction in energy use.
items.note: Common patterns: a reduction in consumption or a reduction of a certain amount.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: Insulation can reduce the amount of energy a building uses.
items.note: Verb: make something smaller or less.

items.section: C · Global and environmental word families
items.example: The revised process operates at a reduced temperature.
items.note: Past participle or adjective from reduce.

items.example: Chemical spills can endanger freshwater wildlife.
items.note: Verb corresponding to the adjective endangered; exercise 24.3 contrasts these forms.

items.pt: descarte de resíduos; destinação de resíduos
items.example: The town introduced a safer waste disposal system.
items.note: A standard compound noun formed in exercise 24.2, related to disposal and dispose of waste.

items.example: The new technology delivered a significant reduction in fuel consumption.
items.note: Common adjective–noun combination used in exercise 24.3.
